query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys reported to date commonly contain both solid solutions and intermetallic compounds. Induction-melted Al- and Mg-rich alloys reached densities of 2.64–2.75 g/cm3 but all had complex structures; Al20Be20Fe10Si15Ti35 combined a density of 3.91 g/cm3 with 911 HV hardness and oxidation resistance at 700 and 900 °C; compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd showed region-dependent compression, plasticity, and corrosion behavior; and reported AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys contained a primary BCC constituent together with intermetallic compounds, with x = 1.0 showing the best property combination in that series. Prior studies have emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, whereas interfacial segregation, interfacial energy, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance remain insufficiently studied. The design must retain a density below 6 g/cm3 and address performance constraints associated with the tendency of Mg and dissimilar constituent elements to form stable intermetallic compounds. Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state, what single intervention hypothesis could improve its combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance? State the intervention, its proposed causal mechanism, quantitative or directional predictions relative to the as-processed baseline, the composition and operating or test boundaries, the prior experimental evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with explicit observations that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a eutectic solidification process to produce a near-equilibrium microstructure with low-energy phase boundaries and regular lamellar organization will improve the combined mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance of the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state
generation.conditions: High temperatures up to the reaction temperature; solidification state
generation.structural_mediator: Near-equilibrium microstructure with low-energy phase boundaries and regular lamellar organization
generation.mechanism: The eutectic solidification process produces a microstructure that resists microstructural change at high temperatures and provides high rupture strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation performance
generation.boundary: Temperature range up to the reaction temperature
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature range and processing conditions required to achieve the desired microstructure are uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the microstructure and performance of the alloy produced by eutectic solidification with that of the as-processed alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the eutectic solidification process does not produce a near-equilibrium microstructure with low-energy phase boundaries and regular lamellar organization, or if the alloy's performance does not improve, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Mechanism with scope. Mechanism: The eutectic solidification process produces near-equilibrium microstructures with low-energy phase boundaries and regular lamellar organization, which resist microstructural change at high temperatures and provide high rupture strength.. System: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) designed with the eutectic alloy concept. Conditions: High temperatures up to the reaction temperature; solidification state. Evidence: inferred. Observation: The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm and showed excellent mechanical properties up to 700°C.. Scope limits: Requires the alloy to be at or near the eutectic composition to achieve the isothermal transformation and avoid solidification temperature ranges.. Alternatives: Non-eutectic HEAs which suffer from inferior castability and compositional segregation.. Quote: "Eutectic alloys are also known to be good candidate high-temperature alloys, because the eutectic solidification structure has the following features: 1) near-equilibrium microstructures that resist change at temperatures as high as their reaction temperature"
